## Why This Matters

Deep networks existed for decades before they worked. The reason they were "mostly abandoned in the
early 2000s" was not a shortage of compute or data alone -- it was that **nobody could train them**.
Stack enough layers and the gradients dissolve on the way down, so the lower layers never move; or
they blow up, and the loss diverges to `NaN`. What rescued deep learning was not one idea but a
**toolkit** of small, sharp fixes, each repairing one failure mode.

The picture to hold: a deep net is a **bucket brigade** passing the error signal hand-to-hand from the
output back to the input. If each handoff spills a little -- a saturating activation, weights at the
wrong scale -- nothing reaches the front of the line. This lesson is the brigade's equipment: better
grips (initialization), non-spilling buckets (ReLU), a foreman who re-levels the line each round
(batch norm), a faster cadence (momentum, Adam), and a rule against over-eager runners (dropout).

## The Disease: Unstable Gradients

Backprop (L16) computes a parameter's gradient by **multiplying local derivatives along the path from
the loss back to that parameter**. In a deep net those paths are long, so the gradient is a long
product of factors. If the typical factor is a bit **less than 1**, the product shrinks geometrically
toward zero by the time it reaches the lowest layers -- the **vanishing-gradients** problem: the lower
layers get almost no signal and barely learn. If the typical factor is a bit **more than 1**, the
product blows up -- the **exploding-gradients** problem, which shows up most in recurrent nets and ends
in divergence. The umbrella name is **unstable gradients**: different layers learn at wildly different
speeds.

```{mermaid}
flowchart RL
  L["loss<br/>grad = 1"] --> o["output layer<br/>grad healthy"]
  o --> h3["hidden 3<br/>x 0.3"]
  h3 --> h2["hidden 2<br/>x 0.3"]
  h2 --> h1["hidden 1<br/>grad ~ 0 (vanished)"]
  h1 --> i["input layer<br/>never learns"]
```

The classic 2010 culprit (Glorot and Bengio): the **sigmoid** activation paired with the then-standard
initialization. Sigmoid **saturates** -- for large positive or negative inputs its output flattens and
its derivative is nearly zero -- and it has a mean of 0.5, not 0. Multiply many near-zero derivatives
together and the signal to the lower layers is gone. The lab makes this concrete: an 8-layer sigmoid
net's first-layer gradient norm is essentially `0.000000`, and its loss never moves off `0.693`
(`= ln 2`, the cost of guessing).

## Cure 1 -- Initialization

Glorot and Bengio's insight: for the signal to flow, the **variance of the activations should stay
roughly constant from layer to layer** (forward), and so should the variance of the gradients
(backward). That pins down how to scale the initial random weights, using a layer's **fan-in** (number
of inputs) and **fan-out** (number of outputs):

| Scheme | Variance scaled by | Use with |
|---|---|---|
| **Glorot / Xavier** | `fan_avg = (fan_in + fan_out)/2` | tanh, sigmoid, linear |
| **He / Kaiming** | `fan_in` | ReLU and its variants |

The mismatch is what bites: Xavier was derived for saturating activations, so on a **ReLU** net it
still lets the signal die. In the lab, passing a signal through 20 ReLU layers gives an activation
std of `0.0000` (PyTorch's plain default), `0.0009` (Xavier -- still vanishing), and `0.8975` (He --
alive). PyTorch's `nn.Linear` already uses a Kaiming-*style* default, but its conservative `a=sqrt(5)`
scaling (inherited from an old leaky-ReLU setting) makes the weights smaller than He-for-ReLU, so it
*also* vanishes in a deep pure-ReLU stack -- which is why you set the scheme explicitly with
`torch.nn.init` (e.g. `nn.init.kaiming_normal_(layer.weight, nonlinearity="relu")`).

## Cure 2 -- Non-saturating Activations

The other half of the 2010 fix was the activation itself. **ReLU** (`max(0, z)`) does not saturate for
positive inputs and is cheap to compute -- the modern default. Its one flaw is the **dying ReLU**: a
unit whose input is negative for every example outputs 0 forever, and since ReLU's gradient is 0 there,
it never recovers. The refinements all address this:

- **Leaky ReLU / PReLU** -- a small slope for `z < 0`, so the unit can never fully die.
- **ELU / SELU** -- smooth, negative-side curves; a pure-MLP SELU stack *self-normalizes*.
- **GELU / Swish / Mish** -- smooth, curved everywhere; the default in modern transformers, at a
  little extra compute.

Practical rule: **start with ReLU** (paired with He init); reach for a variant only when it pays.

## Cure 3 -- Batch Normalization

**Batch normalization** (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015) inserts a step between a layer and its activation
that **normalizes each feature across the mini-batch** to zero mean and unit variance, then applies a
**learnable scale and shift** (gamma, beta) so the network can undo the normalization if it helps.
Keeping activations well-conditioned at every depth stabilizes training, permits **higher learning
rates**, and mildly regularizes. One catch you must respect: BatchNorm uses the **current batch's
statistics during `train()`** but **running averages during `eval()`** -- so the mode you put the model
in matters at inference time.

## Cure 4 -- Better Optimizers

Plain gradient descent takes a step of fixed size `lr` in the direction of the gradient. Two upgrades
make it dramatically faster and more robust:

- **Momentum** -- accumulate a *velocity* from past gradients and step with that. Like a ball rolling
  downhill, it powers through flat spots and damps the zig-zag across narrow valleys.
- **Adam** -- keeps a per-parameter running average of the gradient (momentum) **and** of its squared
  magnitude (RMSProp), and uses them to give **each parameter its own adaptive step size**. It is the
  robust default: it just works without much tuning.

In the lab, on the same net for 150 epochs, the final loss is `0.130` (SGD), `0.056` (SGD + momentum),
and `0.044` (Adam) -- Adam converges fastest with no hand-holding.

::: {.callout-important title="The learning rate is the master dial"}
No optimizer saves you from a bad **learning rate**. Too high and the loss bounces or diverges to
`NaN`; too low and training crawls. The lab's sweep makes it vivid: `lr = 10` ends at loss `4.80`
(diverged), `lr = 0.0001` crawls to `0.42`, and `lr = 0.01` reaches `0.048` (test `0.992`). When a net
will not train, the learning rate is the first knob to turn -- sweep it by orders of magnitude. A
**learning-rate schedule** (step, exponential, or cosine decay) starts large to move fast, then shrinks
to settle into the minimum.
:::

## Cure 5 -- Dropout

Big networks have the capacity to **memorize** the training set (L09's overfitting, now with millions
of parameters). **Dropout** (Srivastava et al., 2014) fights it by **randomly zeroing a fraction `p` of
activations on every training step**, so no unit can lean on any particular other unit -- the net is
forced to spread its bets and learn redundant, robust features. It is the neural-net regularizer named
back in L10, now developed. Like BatchNorm, it is **active in `train()` and switched off in `eval()`**
(at test time you want the whole network). In the lab a wide net memorizes a 20-feature set (train
`1.000`, test `0.840`); adding `nn.Dropout(0.5)` raises test accuracy to `0.880` and shrinks the
train-test gap from `0.160` to `0.120`.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  d["Unstable gradients<br/>(vanish / explode)"] --> c1["Init: Glorot / He"]
  d --> c2["Activation: ReLU & co."]
  d --> c3["Batch normalization"]
  d --> c4["Optimizer: momentum / Adam<br/>+ learning-rate schedule"]
  ov["Overfitting"] --> c5["Dropout"]
```

Each cure repairs one failure mode: the four on the left keep the gradient signal -- the backward pass
from L16 -- flowing through depth, while dropout fights the separate problem of an over-large net
memorizing the training set.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Xavier init on a ReLU net.** The signal dies just like the default -- ReLU wants **He**.
- **Leaving the model in `train()` at evaluation.** Dropout keeps dropping and BatchNorm uses batch
  stats, so your test numbers are wrong. Call `model.eval()` before measuring (and `model.train()`
  before the next training step).
- **A learning rate off by orders of magnitude.** The single most common reason a net "won't train."
  Sweep it first.
- **Reaching for exotic activations or stacking every trick blindly.** ReLU + He + Adam already train
  most nets; add BatchNorm or dropout when a real problem (instability, overfitting) calls for it.
- **"Deeper is always better."** Without these tricks, deeper is often *worse* -- the whole reason this
  lesson exists.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Which optimizer should I actually use?"** -- Start with **Adam** (robust, little tuning). For the
last bit of generalization on big vision models, practitioners often switch to **SGD + momentum** with
a schedule near the end. For most work, Adam is the answer.

**"Do I still need careful init if I use BatchNorm?"** -- BatchNorm makes a net far less sensitive to
initialization, so you can get away with more. But He init + ReLU is free and standard, and not every
architecture uses BatchNorm -- so yes, still init sensibly.

**"ReLU or something fancier?"** -- ReLU is the default and usually fine. Swish/GELU/Mish can give a
small bump on hard tasks at extra compute; leaky ReLU is a cheap insurance against dying units. Don't
agonize -- profile, then decide.

**"How do I pick the learning rate?"** -- Sweep by orders of magnitude (`1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, ...`) and
watch the loss curve, exactly as the lab's Ex1 does; pick the largest rate that trains stably, then add
a decay schedule. The deeper, automated version of this tuning is the CDAT 4013 lab's territory.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Problem / tool | The one-liner |
|---|---|
| Unstable gradients | backprop multiplies local derivatives -> deep products vanish (<1) or explode (>1) |
| Glorot / Xavier init | scale by `fan_avg`; for tanh / sigmoid / linear |
| He / Kaiming init | scale by `fan_in`; for ReLU and variants (the default choice) |
| ReLU & variants | non-saturating activation; leaky/ELU/SELU/GELU fix the dying-ReLU corner |
| Batch normalization | normalize each feature per batch + learnable scale/shift; batch stats in train, running in eval |
| Momentum | a velocity over past gradients -- faster, smoother descent |
| Adam | per-parameter adaptive step sizes (momentum + RMSProp); the robust default |
| Learning rate | the master dial: too high diverges, too low crawls; decay it on a schedule |
| Dropout | randomly zero a fraction of activations each step -> regularizes; off at eval |
